title: Electrician
description: Install, maintain and repair domestic and light-industrial electrical systems. Read wiring diagrams, test circuits, diagnose faults, and work to the wiring regulations. Safety and correct earthing are not negotiable.
questions: Walk me through wiring a single-phase domestic distribution board.
A ceiling fan runs slowly on every regulator setting. How do you diagnose it?
What is earthing for, and how would you test whether an earth is good?
Explain the difference between an MCB and an RCD, and when you'd use each.
You measure 230 V between live and neutral but the appliance won't run. What next?
What PPE do you put on before opening a live board, and why each item?
reference: Every candidate should be able to state, unprompted: isolate, lock off, and TEST DEAD before touching any conductor — proving the tester on a known live source, testing the conductor, then proving the tester again. Earthing exists so fault current has a low-resistance path and the protective device operates; a high-resistance earth is a dangerous earth, not a weak one. An MCB protects the CIRCUIT from overload and short circuit; an RCD protects the PERSON from earth leakage. They are not substitutes.

title: Line Cook
description: Work a station on a busy service line. Prep to spec, cook to order, plate consistently, and keep the station clean and within food-safety limits under time pressure.
questions: Talk me through setting up your mise en place before a dinner service.
What are the safe internal temperatures for chicken, beef and fish?
You're four tickets behind and the pass is calling. What do you do?
Explain the danger zone and how you keep prepped food out of it.
A dish comes back to the kitchen. Walk me through your response.
How do you prevent cross-contamination when you're moving fast?
reference: Poultry to 74 °C, ground meat 71 °C, whole cuts 63 °C, fish 63 °C. The danger zone is 5–60 °C; food should not sit in it beyond four hours cumulatively. Colour-coded boards and a sanitiser bucket within reach are the two habits that prevent most cross-contamination. A returned dish is remade, not argued about — the response the interviewer is listening for is ownership plus a check of whether the whole batch is affected.
